rationale: Qualitative case study (key-informant interviews, semi-structured interviews with water sellers and users, Blantyre Water Board questionnaires, municipal records, and newspaper content analysis) examining water kiosk governance in Nkolokoti Township, Blantyre, Malawi. The central empirical focus critiques community participation through locally elected water committees (CDCs, water selling committees, and Nkhomano Health and Sanitation Committees; participation_assistance), while co-equally analyzing multi-stakeholder institutional mandates and decentralization failures across the Blantyre City Assembly, Blantyre Water Board, ward councillors, and MPs (institutional_structure_coordination), comparing direct utility-managed vs community-committee-managed kiosk models (regulatory_model_ownership), and examining utility mass disconnections of kiosks for unpaid bill arrears (enforcement_sanctions) alongside kiosk vs private-tap pricing (fees_tariffs_subsidies). Outcomes co-equally center on functional sustainability, continuity, and safe water access for low-income households (effective_access), kiosk governance, revenue arrears, and disconnection incidence (administrative_outcome), and affordability/price burdens when kiosk cutoffs force reliance on higher-priced private taps (economic_access).
